opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest lesson is about timing and conviction. NVIDIA has a habit of betting on things years before they're obvious. CUDA was a bet on general-purpose GPU computing long before deep learning took off, and for a while people thought it was a strange use of resources. Then AlexNet happened, and suddenly that bet looked like foresight. Humanoid robotics and embodied AI feel similar to me. The question isn't whether it works perfectly today. The question is whether the curve is bending in the right direction, and I believe it is.

The second lesson is to think in terms of the full stack. When we started the GEAR lab, the goal wasn't just to build one cool robot demo. It was to ask what the foundation model for robotics looks like, and what you need underneath it: simulation, synthetic data, compute, and the hardware partners building the actual bodies. A lot of founders focus on one layer. But in a new field where the infrastructure doesn't exist yet, sometimes you have to build the picks and shovels and the gold mine at the same time.

Third, data is the real moat, and in robotics it's the hardest problem. Language models had the whole internet to train on. Robots don't have an internet of physical actions. So you have to get creative. You combine real teleoperation data, which is expensive and doesn't scale well, with simulation, which scales infinitely but has a reality gap, and with internet video, which shows you how the world works but not the motor commands. Whoever figures out how to blend those data sources well will have a huge advantage. For founders, that means asking early: what's my data flywheel, and why can't someone else just copy it?

And finally, why humanoids specifically? The world is built for the human form. Our factories, homes, tools, and stairs are all designed around two arms, two legs, and a certain height. If you want one general-purpose robot that can go anywhere and use anything, the humanoid form factor makes a lot of sense. There's also a data argument. There's a massive amount of video of humans doing things, and a humanoid body maps more naturally onto that.

So my advice to founders is this: find the problem that will be enormous in five to ten years, be honest about what's still missing, and be willing to build those missing pieces yourself. Embodied AI is going to be one of those moments, and I think we'll look back on this period the way we now look back on the early days of deep learning.

r001.rationale: The response urges founders to build for embodied AI’s expected importance in five to ten years, but it does not clearly predict that intelligent robots will become ubiquitous.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that it wasn't really one decision. People look at NVIDIA from the outside and see a big announcement at GTC with a lineup of humanoids on stage, and they assume there was some moment where Jensen said, "robots, go." It didn't work that way. It was a sequence of smaller, somewhat unglamorous bets that compounded. We built Isaac Sim years before anyone cared about humanoids. We did the Omniverse work. We did Eureka and VIMA and Voyager, and a lot of that looked like academic curiosity at the time. So lesson one for founders is that the bet that looks bold in retrospect is usually just a long series of boring bets that you refused to abandon.

The second thing I'd say is about timing and conviction, and they're in tension. Jensen has this phrase about working on problems that are "zero billion dollar markets." Humanoid robotics was exactly that. There was no revenue, no customers, and a lot of very smart people would tell you the hardware wasn't ready and the data didn't exist. And they were right, in a narrow sense. But the thing we saw was that the ingredients were converging. Foundation models were getting good at understanding video and language, simulation was getting photorealistic enough to transfer, and the hardware cost curve for actuators and batteries was finally bending. When three or four curves are bending at the same time, you don't wait until it's obvious, because by then there's no advantage left.

Now, I want to be honest about the part founders should not copy. NVIDIA could afford to be early because we have a massive core business that pays for the research. A startup doesn't have that luxury. So the question for a founder is not "should I bet on robotics," it's "which specific layer of this stack can I win in the next eighteen months while the rest of the ecosystem catches up?" Maybe that's data collection. Maybe it's a particular manipulation skill. Maybe it's teleoperation infrastructure. Trying to build the whole vertical as a seed-stage company is how you end up with a very expensive demo video and no company.

The third lesson, and this is the one I feel most strongly about, is to pick the problem where the data flywheel is defensible. For language models, the internet was the free lunch. Everyone got the same text. For robotics, there is no internet of physical actions. Every bit of embodied data has to be generated, in simulation, through teleop, through video. That's painful, but it also means whoever builds the machine that produces that data has a real moat. At NVIDIA we made a bet that simulation plus synthetic data plus a small amount of real-world grounding is the path, and we built GR00T around that philosophy. A founder might disagree with that bet, and that's fine. But you need a thesis about where your data comes from and why nobody else can get it as cheaply.

And one more thing, more of a cultural point. The humanoid form factor itself was a contrarian choice. A lot of roboticists said it's inefficient, why give a machine two legs when wheels work. The argument for it is that the world is built for humans, so a human-shaped body gets to reuse the entire built environment and the entire corpus of human video as training signal. That's a bet on generality over efficiency. And I think the meta-lesson is: when you're deciding what to build, ask what the general-purpose version looks like, even if the specialized version is more sensible today. The specialized thing wins the first customer. The general thing wins the decade. Jensen is willing to lose the first customer. Most founders can't afford to, so they have to find the narrow wedge that still points at the general goal.

r001.rationale: The response argues that converging technology curves make robotics worth pursuing early, but it does not present the anticipated future ubiquity of intelligent robots as the reason to begin working on robotics today.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest lesson is to have a long-term thesis, but make sure every step toward it creates something useful. Humanoid robotics is a long bet. You need intelligence, you need hardware, and you need those two things to work together in a messy physical world. A great demo is only the beginning.

For a founder, I’d ask: what can you build today that becomes more valuable as that future arrives? Maybe it’s simulation, maybe it’s a way to collect better robot data, maybe it’s a system that performs one useful task reliably. You need a concrete starting point and a way to learn from deployment.

And you have to understand your own advantages. A startup shouldn’t copy NVIDIA’s breadth. Pick a problem where you can move faster, get close to users, and build something they actually need. Think big about where the technology is going, and be very specific about what you can deliver next.

r001.rationale: The response recommends building useful robotics capabilities now for a future where the technology advances, but it does not say intelligent robots are expected to become ubiquitous.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest lesson is to have conviction about a long-term direction, but be very concrete about what you need to build today to get there. With embodied AI, the vision is a machine that can perceive, reason, and act in the physical world. But you don’t get there just by deciding to build a humanoid. You need simulation, data, learning algorithms, compute, and a way to evaluate whether the robot is actually getting better.

For a founder, that means asking: What becomes the bottleneck if this future happens? And can I start solving that bottleneck now? Maybe it’s generating training data. Maybe it’s making deployment more reliable. You don’t have to build the entire stack to build something essential.

The other lesson is to distinguish the long-term thesis from the particular implementation. You can be very confident that AI will increasingly interact with the physical world while remaining flexible about which robot designs or learning methods will work best. Have conviction in the destination, and let experiments guide the route.

r001.rationale: The response recommends solving embodied-AI bottlenecks now and predicts more AI interaction with the physical world, but it does not clearly say intelligent robots will become ubiquitous.
